title: B-Tree vs LSM Tree
plainSentence: A lesson with two small database engines side by side that lets you stream in keys and count every page each engine writes and reads.
pitch: Keys stream into two tiny storage engines at once. A B-tree finds the page a key belongs to and rewrites that whole page, while an LSM tree holds writes in a memory waiting room, flushes them as sorted runs and merges runs later. Live counters for pages written and pages read show who pays where, and a Compact control lets the visitor watch levels merge, so they leave knowing why no engine is free. All counts come from the page's own simplified simulation, not from a real database.
firstMinute: The page opens with both engines already ingesting a sample stream of 20 keys, and two running tallies of pages written and pages read side by side. In the first 30 seconds the visitor sees one key light up the page it rewrites in the B-tree, and the same key sit in memory in the LSM tree. The first success is watching the write counters diverge, with no reading needed.
conceptsToLearn: A key-value store keeps values that you look up by key
Disks read and write data in whole fixed-size pages
whyNow: Timeless: engineers choose between B-tree and LSM-based databases every week, and most explanations show only finished diagrams where the costs stay invisible.

purposeDetail.concept: A B-tree storage engine finds the leaf page a key belongs to and rewrites that whole fixed-size page in place, splitting pages when they fill. An LSM tree buffers writes in a memory table, flushes it as an immutable sorted run, and later merges runs into larger levels in a step called compaction. Both engines pay: the B-tree in whole-page rewrites per small write, the LSM tree in repeated rewrites during compaction (write amplification) and in checking several runs on reads (read amplification).
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations show a finished tree diagram or a table of pros and cons, so the costs stay invisible: nobody sees one small write turn into many bytes rewritten, or a read fan out across several runs.
purposeDetail.audience: Programmers who must pick or tune a database and have heard 'LSM is for writes, B-tree is for reads' without seeing why.
prerequisites: What a key and a value are
That disks and SSDs read and write in blocks called pages
misconceptions: A write happens once, at its final place on disk (compaction rewrites the same data several times).
An in-place B-tree update is cheap because it touches only the changed record (the whole page is rewritten).
LSM writes are cheap because they are sequential, so there is no hidden cost (compaction and multi-run reads pay later).
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: The visitor bursts a second wave of keys into both engines and watches the counters cross: the LSM tree wrote little at first, then compaction rewrites the same keys again and again, while the B-tree rewrote a whole page per tiny update. Every engine pays somewhere, and the choice is only about where.
demos: Rung 1, the familiar: a sorted shelf of index cards. Insert one key and see why sorted order helps lookups.
Rung 2, B-tree: stream keys in; each one finds its leaf page and the whole page lights up as rewritten; watch a page split when full and count pages written.
Rung 3, LSM tree: the same keys enter a memory waiting room (the memtable); when it fills it flushes as one sorted run; counters show far fewer page writes so far.
Rung 4, the read side: look up a key and count pages checked in each engine; the LSM tree may check several runs, with a Bloom-filter switch that skips runs.
Rung 5, compaction: press Compact and watch runs merge into the next level, rewriting keys that were already written; the amplification ratio counter climbs.
Rung 6, the dials: choose a workload (random keys, sequential keys, overwrites of hot keys) and a size ratio, and see which engine pays where; page size stays fixed in the simulation.
checkQuestions: You overwrite the same key 100 times. Roughly how many times is that key's data written in each engine, and where?
Why can a read in the LSM tree touch more pages than a read in the B-tree?
What does compaction buy, and what does it cost?
Which workload would make you pick each engine?

research.summary: Re-checked by search on 2026-10-14; no page opened. The 1996 LSM-tree paper (O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick, O'Neil, Acta Informatica 33, pages 351 to 385) is confirmed by the publisher's page and an author-hosted copy; its abstract describes batching index changes in memory and cascading them to disk components. Cassandra's own documentation states that compaction merges small sorted tables into a new one, creating write amplification, and that reads use Bloom filters to skip tables. The authors' own page for the RUM conjecture states that optimising two of read, update and memory overheads costs the third. Weaker, unverified: the B-tree whole-page rewrite cost (TiKV's comparison page appeared in two searches but its text was seen only through summaries), and the 10 to 30 times figure for leveled compaction (a third-party mirror page only). The scout's RocksDB blog claim of 20 to 30 times was not found again. Every counter on the page comes from the page's own deterministic simulation with tiny pages, labelled as a simplified model rather than a benchmark.

facts.claim: The LSM-tree paper by O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick and O'Neil appeared in Acta Informatica 33(4), pages 351 to 385, in 1996; its abstract describes deferring and batching index changes in memory and cascading them to disk components, saving disk-arm movement compared with B-trees for insert-heavy workloads.

Per Cassandra's documentation, compaction reads several small sorted tables, merges them, processes updates and deletes, and writes a new table, which is a source of write amplification; reads merge disk tables with the memtable and use Bloom filters to skip tables that cannot hold the key.

An access method that bounds two of read, update and memory overheads forces a lower bound on the third (the RUM conjecture, EDBT 2016); B-trees are usually described as read-friendly and level-based LSM trees as update-friendly at some cost to reads.

Reported, unverified: in a B-tree a small record update rewrites its whole fixed-size page and a full page splits into several writes, so write amplification grows with page size (TiKV comparison page, via search summaries). The page's simulation defines this behaviour itself with 4 keys per page.

As of 2026-10-14, per a third-party mirror of RocksDB documentation, leveled compaction with a size ratio of 10 is roughly 10 to 30 times write amplification; the scout's 20 to 30 times from the RocksDB blog was not found again. A rough model is size ratio times (levels minus one).
As of 2026-10-14, per one benchmark write-up, random-key writes gave about 4.56 times write amplification and sequential keys about 1.03 times, so amplification depends heavily on key order.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: pick a workload, stream keys into both engines, watch the page-written and page-read counters, then predict the next number before pressing Compact or Look up. The loop stays interesting because each workload (random, sequential, hot overwrites) shifts which engine pays and where, and the visitor's guess is scored against the simulation.
sophisticationHooks: Both engines are simulated in plain code with a fixed small page size (say 4 keys per page), so every count is exact and checkable by a script against hand-worked examples.
Animated pages: a rewritten page flashes, a split pulls apart, runs slide down levels and merge, with a reduced-motion twin that steps instead of animating.
A running 'write amplification' and 'read amplification' dial for each engine, plus a ledger chart over time that makes the compaction spikes visible.
Predict-then-reveal check questions and three workload presets that end in the aha: the counters cross.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: a deterministic B-tree simulator (insert, split, lookup) and a leveled LSM simulator (memtable, flush, level merge) with page counters, 4 keys per page; SVG rendering side by side; three workload presets, play, step and compact controls; intro, explainer and four check questions. Stretch only if time remains: Bloom-filter switch and a size-ratio dial. Cut: deletes and tombstones, tiered compaction, page-size dial, concurrency, crash recovery, real timing or hardware claims, persistence.
risks: The B-tree whole-page rewrite fact and every amplification multiplier are unverified (blended summaries, single third-party pages): the page defines its own simplified model and shows reported figures only as 'as of 2026-10-14, per <source>' or omits them.
The 'a write happens once' misconception is not documented as a widely held belief by any source seen: the page frames it as a common assumption to test, not as a survey finding.
The aha 'the counters cross' depends on tuned presets: the simulators need scripted tests that confirm the crossing for the overwrite and burst presets, otherwise the claim is reworded.
Simulated counts depend on page size and size ratio and are not benchmarks: the page says so plainly and never claims real database speeds.
Scope is tight for one morning (two engines plus animation): build and test both simulators first, with a stepped reduced-motion twin instead of animation if time runs short.

The RocksDB blog, Aerospike, candost and one other blog source from the scout were not found again and are dropped; the page cites only the Springer paper, the Cassandra documentation and the RUM page as verified.

verification.notes: The LSM paper, Cassandra compaction behaviour and the RUM trade-off rest on primary pages; the B-tree page-rewrite cost and all multipliers stay unverified and are demoted to the page's own labelled simulation. Feasible only with the shrunk scope (leveled LSM, fixed page size).
